quest_010_00.story:
At the edge of white stone ossuaries, Shen Ning waits until the last lantern is lit before speaking. Shen Ning is known as a spirit gardener, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Shen Ning has brought the bronze bell clapper, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect a village burned under a false imperial order to the curse spreading through Bone Meridian. Shen Ning asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Shen Ning explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Bone Meridian, where a necropolis where the dead are forced to pay rent. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Su Xuan remembers the night differently. Su Xuan heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The ancestral council later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Shen Ning wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called A Name in Water. Its immediate task is speak with Shen Ning. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Shen Ning insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Dawn Sanctuary follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Shen Ning gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Su Xuan explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Bone Meridian in the first place.

The creature called Bone Hound appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of charge. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Shen Ning once trusted the ancestral council because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Su Xuan asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns a village burned under a false imperial order. Shen Ning has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Shen Ning chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near white stone ossuaries. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Shen Ning recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Bone Hound, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Su Xuan proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Shen Ning refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Shen Ning teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Dawn Sanctuary arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises truth without humiliation while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Su Xuan has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Shen Ning speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Bone Hound senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of speak with Shen Ning cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Su Xuan asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Shen Ning gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The bronze bell clapper now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Shen Ning wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through white stone ossuaries with the result of speak with Shen Ning. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Shen Ning records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Shen Ning offers a conversation rather than another command. Shen Ning asks Lin Yue whether truth without humiliation can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Bone Meridian, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Su Xuan receives a copy, Shen Ning retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: Its ribs are the missing temple steps where refugees waited for shelter that never opened.
quest_010_00.mercy: Shen Ning records the result of the task to speak with Shen Ning. The account is witnessed rather than final: Su Xuan receives a copy, and the next chapter follows the evidence carried by the bronze bell clapper. The binding's final fate remains undecided.

Bai Jin is known as a memory smith, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Bai Jin has brought the stormglass seal, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect an apprentice trapped inside an unfinished ritual to the curse spreading through Bone Meridian. Bai Jin asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Bai Jin explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Bone Meridian, where a necropolis where the dead are forced to pay rent. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Yun Suyin remembers the night differently. Yun Suyin heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The ancestral council later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Bai Jin wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called The Road of Missing Bells. Its immediate task is visit Jade Academy and observe its meridian. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Bai Jin insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Jade Academy follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Bai Jin gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Yun Suyin explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Bone Meridian in the first place.

The creature called Pearl Spirit appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of charge. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Bai Jin once trusted the ancestral council because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Yun Suyin asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns an apprentice trapped inside an unfinished ritual. Bai Jin has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Bai Jin chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near white stone ossuaries. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Bai Jin recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Pearl Spirit, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Yun Suyin proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Bai Jin refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Bai Jin teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Jade Academy arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises justice without revenge while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Yun Suyin has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Bai Jin speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Pearl Spirit senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of visit Jade Academy and observe its meridian cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Yun Suyin asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Bai Jin gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The stormglass seal now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Bai Jin wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through white stone ossuaries with the result of visit Jade Academy and observe its meridian. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Bai Jin records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Bai Jin offers a conversation rather than another command. Bai Jin asks Lin Yue whether justice without revenge can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Bone Meridian, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Yun Suyin receives a copy, Bai Jin retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: The pearl formed around the last breath of a diver who was ordered to recover tribute during a storm.
quest_058_02.mercy: Bai Jin records the result of the task to visit Jade Academy and observe its meridian. The account is witnessed rather than final: Yun Suyin receives a copy, and the next chapter follows the evidence carried by the stormglass seal. The binding's final fate remains undecided.

Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The ancestral council later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Yun Lian wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called What We Owe the Living. Its immediate task is speak with Shen Rui. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Yun Lian insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Dream Orchard follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Yun Lian gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Shen Rui explains it. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Bone Meridian in the first place.

The creature called Pearl Spirit appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Yun Lian once trusted the ancestral council because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

The danger returns when Pearl Spirit senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.
